content: Homer is a headless personal AI daemon that runs continuously on a Mac Mini and exposes its state through controlled interfaces.
The public portfolio describes Homer as a personal AI operating system rather than a generic chatbot interface.
Homer stores operational facts, decisions, lessons, insights, questions, and commitments as structured claims.
Operational claims live in SQLite with FTS5 indexing, while preference claims also mirror to durable markdown files.
The memory layer deliberately separates canonical storage from the live retrieval context used during an interaction.
Homer uses SQLite plus FTS5 instead of relying on a separate vector database alone because lexical truth, local durability, and semantic recall need to be fused.
The retrieval stack fuses lexical BM25 ranks with vector ranks using reciprocal rank fusion.
Homer's public ranking constants use an RRF rank offset of 20 for hybrid retrieval fusion.
Vector search in Homer applies a cosine similarity floor of 0.40 before a semantic result can enter fusion.
Homer's recency multiplier has a 90 day half-life and a 0.75 floor so old durable claims are demoted but not erased.
Approved claims receive a stronger tier multiplier when the query contains an entity that appears in the claim.
Candidate claims are intentionally demoted in retrieval until a human review path promotes them.
Archived claims stay searchable at a lower score so the system can show stale context without treating it as current truth.
Homer's conflict guard sends semantically similar or contradictory high-impact memory changes to human review instead of auto-merging them.
The conflict path exists because appending a correction without retiring the stale claim can leave old status live in retrieval.
Homer treats markdown as a human-readable surface, not as the full operational mirror of the claim database.
The memory architecture evolved through production retrieval failures rather than being chosen as a finished design upfront.
Homer's public page states that the memory layer indexes 24.7 GB of data.
The architecture panel reports 12,481 stored claims in the public Homer demo.
The nightly memory consolidation trace describes extracting durable claims, superseding stale rows, and rebuilding FTS5 plus vector indices.
Homer uses Gemini embedding-001 for semantic memory vectors and stores a 768 dimension prefix for retrieval.
Document embeddings use a retrieval-document task while query embeddings use a retrieval-query task.
Homer routes memory search through an MCP tool so different harnesses can share the same retrieval behavior.
Memory freshness checks are required before Homer answers about current status, goals, plans, commitments, or preferences.
The memory scribe queues inferred durable facts for human review instead of silently approving every observation.
Homer's scheduler runs cron-style jobs from hot-reloadable schedule files.
The public Homer hero presents 48 daily scheduled tasks as a static system figure.
The default scheduled job set includes morning brief, memory rollup, idea review, link processing, idea exploration, and planning reminders.
Homer's scheduler is designed to survive normal macOS sleep and wake cycles on the host machine.
Scheduler failures are expected to escalate loudly instead of disappearing inside a silent background loop.
The morning routine demo shows the morning brief as job 01 of 48 in the daemon schedule.
A morning brief run pulls overnight memory deltas and active commitments, then Claude drafts the brief before Codex verifies the sanitized output.
The morning routine includes calendar and weather fetches before composing a brief.
A verifier step checks the sanitized morning brief before it is delivered through the notification path.
The link processor classifies queued URLs by type before routing them into the idea pipeline.
The public README describes nightly link processing as a route from captured links into ideas, plans, and execution.
Homer runs with a single-instance launchd daemon and a flock guard to avoid duplicate background workers.
The launchd install renders a plist from a template rather than hard-coding host-specific paths.
Homer loads secrets from an environment file and does not place credentials inside the launchd plist.
The public repo is reference material and deliberately excludes private subsystems and personal data.
The portfolio frontend is a prerendered Vite application deployed through Cloudflare Pages.
The portfolio backend runs FastAPI behind a Cloudflare Tunnel on the Mac Mini Docker host.
Redis provides rate limiting and ephemeral shared state for the portfolio backend.
Supabase stores durable data for selected portfolio workflows, while the Homer memory demo uses only a static corpus.
The Cloudflare Pages BFF forwards request IDs and trusted client IP headers to the FastAPI backend.
The portfolio backend uses one gunicorn worker for stateful stream coordination in the Fortune workflow.
Homer exposes Telegram, telephony webhooks, and MCP stdio as entry points rather than opening a broad public HTTP API.
The public README describes telephony as Homer's only public HTTP surface.
Telephony call-complete webhooks are signed and persist transcripts before returning success.
Twilio SMS webhooks are signed and then relayed into the owner-facing notification channel.
ElevenLabs Managed Agent was chosen over a custom STT and TTS stack after custom voice pipelines proved operationally fragile.
The voice lesson is that managed infrastructure can beat a custom stack when reliability matters more than owning every component.
The public architecture panel frames voice as a phone for agents, including hands-free access and critical failure calls.
Voice v2 on the roadmap focuses on interruption and full-duplex barge-in.
Homer uses five CLI executors in the public page: Claude, Codex, Gemini, Kimi, and opencode.
Executor routing lets Homer pick the cheapest capable model for a task instead of binding the system to one vendor.
The executor layer can route deep reasoning to Codex, web-search research to Gemini, long context to Kimi, and default work to Claude.
The executor subsystem is designed to survive provider outages by rerouting work when a provider hangs.
The public architecture receipts list five executors and a 99.4 percent success rate.
Executor selection is a routing problem over cost, latency, context length, tool access, and failure mode.
Homer centralizes tool access behind an MCP server so every harness can use the same capabilities.
The MCP server registers memory, blob, idea, plan, todo, call, preference, and session tools.
A single MCP tool gateway avoids rewriting the same integration separately for each CLI agent.
The public architecture page describes the MCP layer as centralized permissions, logs, and capability parity.
Homer's web UI is a window into the daemon state, while the daemon remains the source of behavior.
The web UI uses the same backend as the CLI-facing system instead of presenting a separate mock layer.
The Try Homer section is built as telemetry and archived operation traces, not as a free-form chat box.
The archived self-pruning trace shows Homer proposing deletion of an unused skill after observing zero recent invocations.
The skills lesson is that a system for adding capabilities also needs a system for deleting capabilities that no longer pay rent.
Homer's skills harness tracks invocation patterns so unused skills can be flagged before they bloat the working context.
The roadmap includes a public Try Homer console that runs sanitized commands against a public-safe view.
The roadmap includes homer-lite as an MIT-licensed architecture extraction without personal data or production secrets.
The roadmap includes a self-pruning skills harness that proposes merges and consolidations, not just deletions.
Cross-device memory sync is listed as a future thin remote client that pushes claims over an encrypted tunnel.
A marketplace of agent recipes is listed as a future registry of named flows installable into a Homer instance.
Homer's public positioning is proof that production agents need durable memory, orchestration, scheduled work, and tool boundaries.
The architecture extraction should show real mechanisms rather than hiding behind vague agent-platform language.
The public demo should disclose when vector embedding is unavailable instead of pretending hybrid search ran.
The Homer page visual system uses a terminal aesthetic, JetBrains Mono, warm gold accents, and dark pane chrome.
The hero boot sequence is presentational; its static boot values describe the system rather than a live private data snapshot.
The live uptime badge is wired to a public metrics JSON file because that number can safely grow over time.
The public morning routine is a sanitized terminal replay, not a live stream of private calendar or memory contents.
The morning routine video file was retired because a missing media path could be answered by the SPA fallback as HTML.
The portfolio architecture keeps SSR and prerendering as verification boundaries for the Homer page.
The public memory search endpoint is read-only and should never write to the real Homer database.
The public memory search corpus should contain claims about Homer itself, not claims copied from private memory.
A static corpus makes the retrieval demo auditable in a public GitHub repository.
A scoring trace is more credible than a plain answer because it exposes BM25 rank, cosine similarity, RRF, tier, recency, and final score.
The public retrieval demo should cap query length and reject HTML because it is exposed to anonymous visitors.
The public retrieval demo should rate limit anonymous users by IP to protect the Gemini embedding endpoint.
Candidate memory rows are useful in a demo because they make the tier multiplier visible in traces.
A candidate claim suggests that future versions may add diversity demotion to the public memory search trace.
A candidate claim suggests that the public console could later expose sanitized MCP tool calls after the memory search proves safe.
A candidate claim says the retrieval UI may add side-by-side lexical and vector candidate lists for teaching purposes.
A candidate claim says the hourly public search quota may be tuned after traffic data exists.
A candidate claim says the memory demo could later stream partial retrieval traces if request latency becomes noticeable.
An archived design used a metrics section with placeholder tiles before the Homer page was simplified.
An archived proof strip duplicated credibility one-liners that later moved into the hero boot block.
An archived memory design treated markdown as a fuller compatibility mirror before structured claims became the canonical store.
An archived voice approach explored custom STT and TTS plumbing before the managed agent path became the production choice.
Homer prefers SQLite for durable local state over introducing a hosted vector database when hybrid retrieval can stay in-process.
Homer prefers cheap, fast executors for discovery and batch work, reserving deeper models for coding and verification.
Public tool interactions prefer explicit typed arguments and exact allowlists over natural-language tool selection.
Homer interface motion prefers Framer Motion spring physics for responsive transitions instead of decorative constant-speed animation.
Destructive operations prefer explicit Telegram approval before any delete can proceed.
Public runtime access prefers a narrow read-only host bridge over mounting the live SQLite database into application containers.
Public demos prefer an honestly labeled recorded replay when a live dependency is unavailable rather than presenting stale data as live.
